description: Per-translation glossary overlay for the Wheel of Heaven Translation of 2 Kings (wave A, the Elijah cycle: chapters 1, 2). v1.0.0 (2026-11-01, Editor pass, claude-opus-5-5) creates the overlay. It holds nine conventions shared verbatim with the 1-kings-woh overlay (Hebrew proper-name transliteration, the elohim referent/article rule, the 'man of the Elohim' title, the nefesh scope and spelling, the ruach transliteration, Ketiv/Qere, the MT baseline at versional cruxes and versification, 'YHWH of hosts', and Ba'al) and four 2 Kings-specific decisions (Ba'al-Zevuv of Eqron, the sons of the prophets, the double portion of 2:9, and the chariot and horses of fire of 2:11-12). Shared entries carry identical text and appliesTo in both overlays; extend both together. v1.1.0 (2026-11-01, mirrored from the 1-kings-woh Editor pass for Kings wave B, 1 Kgs 1, 2, 13, 22): eight shared entries extended (names, nefesh, man of the Elohim, elohim referent, Ketiv/Qere, MT baseline, Ba'al, ruach) with 1 Kings refIds and wave-B clauses; no 2 Kings rendering changes. v1.2.0 (2026-11-01, Editor pass, Kings waves C-D: 1 Kgs 6, 8; 2 Kgs 4, 17) adds one 2 Kings-specific decision (mišpāṭ 'manner', 2 Kgs 17:26-40) and two shared entries (gāhar 'crouched'; tôrâ 'law'), extends seven shared entries (names, elohim referent incl. new clause 5, man of the Elohim, nefesh, Ketiv/Qere, MT baseline, Ba'al) and the 2 Kings entry bene-ha-neviim (4:1, 38); shared changes mirrored in 1-kings-woh v1.2.0.

entries.source: אֵלִיָּהוּ / אֵלִיָּה ; אַחְאָב ; אִיזֶבֶל ; אֲחַזְיָהוּ / אֲחַזְיָה ...

entries.lemma: Hebrew personal names and toponyms of the Elijah-Elisha narratives (1 Kgs 17 - 2 Kgs 2 and following)
entries.partOfSpeech: proper nouns (personal names, divine names of foreign deities, toponyms) - book-wide rendering convention
entries.literal: the Hebrew name forms as written in the Masoretic Text
entries.standardEnglish: the conventional English (KJV/ASV) forms: Elijah, Ahab, Jezebel, Obadiah, Carmel, Baal, Jezreel, Samaria, Jordan, Israel ...
entries.wohChoice: WoH transliteration of the Hebrew name (Eliyahu, Ach'av, Izevel, Ovadyahu, Karmel, Ba'al, Yizre'el, Shomron, Yarden, Yisra'el ...), normalized to the long theophoric form where the MT alternates (ʾēliyyâ / ʾēliyyāhû -> Eliyahu; ʾăḥazyâ / ʾăḥazyāhû -> Achazyahu); a small set of names fixed in English usage is kept in English (Moab, Aram, Damascus, Horeb, Gilgal). Equivalence table: Eliyahu = Elijah; Elisha = Elisha; Ach'av = Ahab; Achazyahu = Ahaziah; Izevel = Jezebel; Ovadyahu = Obadiah; Chaza'el = Hazael; Yehu = Jehu; Nimshi = Nimshi; Shafat = Shaphat; Yehoram = Jehoram; Yehoshafat = Jehoshaphat; Ba'al = Baal; Ba'al-Zevuv = Baal-zebub; Karmel = Carmel; Kerit = Cherith; Qishon = Kishon; Shomron = Samaria; Tzarfat = Zarephath; Tzidon = Sidon; Gil'ad = Gilead; Yarden = Jordan; Yizre'el = Jezreel; Avel-Mecholah = Abel-meholah; Eqron = Ekron; Yericho = Jericho; Beit-El = Bethel; Be'er Sheva = Beersheba; Yisra'el = Israel; Yehudah = Judah; Avraham = Abraham; Yitzchaq = Isaac; Ya'aqov = Jacob. Kept in their familiar English form: Moab, Aram, Damascus, Horeb, Gilgal, Asherah, and the gentilic 'Tishbite'. Wave B (1 Kgs 1, 2, 13, 22): Shelomoh = Solomon; Adoniyahu = Adonijah (MT short form ʾăḏōniyyâ at 1:5, 7, 18; 2:28, normalized); Tzidqiyahu = Zedekiah (short form ṣiḏqiyyâ at 22:11, normalized); Bat-Sheva = Bathsheba; Natan = Nathan; Tzadoq = Zadok; Benayahu = Benaiah; Yehoyada = Jehoiada; Yo'av = Joab; Tzeruyah = Zeruiah; Evyatar = Abiathar; Avishag = Abishag; Chaggit = Haggith; Avshalom = Absalom; Yonatan = Jonathan; Shim'i = Shimei; Re'i = Rei; Avner = Abner; Yeter = Jether; Gera = Gera; Barzillai = Barzillai; Bachurim = Bahurim; Machanayim = Mahanaim; Hevron = Hebron; Gihon = Gihon; Ein-Rogel = En-rogel; Zochelet = Zoheleth; Anatot = Anathoth; Qidron = Kidron; Akhish = Achish; Ma'akhah = Maacah; Gat = Gath; Yerushalayim = Jerusalem; Moshe = Moses; Yarov'am = Jeroboam; Nevat = Nebat; Yoshiyahu = Josiah; Mikhayehu = Micaiah; Yimlah = Imlah; Kena'anah = Chenaanah; Ramot-Gil'ad = Ramoth-gilead; Yo'ash = Joash; Azuvah = Azubah; Shilchi = Shilhi; Etzyon-Gever = Ezion-geber. Kept in English: Edom, Ophir, Tarshish, Asa, Amon, David. Tsade is written tz (Tzarfat, Tzidon, Tzadoq, Tzidqiyahu, Etzyon-Gever). Gentilics in -î take English '-ite' on the transliterated stem: the Tishbite, the Shunammite, the Gil'adite, the Binyaminite, and the collectives hakkərēṯî wəhappəlēṯî 'the Kerethites and the Pelethites'. Hevron and Gihon keep the genesis-woh spellings. Waves C-D (1 Kgs 6, 8; 2 Kgs 4, 17): Mitzrayim = Egypt; Tziyyon = Zion; Chamat = Hamath; month names Ziv (later Iyyar), Bul (later Marcheshvan), Etanim = Ethanim (later Tishri); Gechazi = Gehazi; Shunem = Shunem; Ba'al-Shalishah = Baal-shalishah; Achaz = Ahaz; Hoshea = Hoshea; Elah = Elah; Shalman'eser = Shalmaneser; Ashur = Assyria; So = So; Par'oh = Pharaoh; Chalach = Halah; Chavor = Habor; Gozan = Gozan; Madai = the Medes; Bavel = Babylon; Kutah / Kut = Cuthah / Cuth (both MT forms kept); Avva = Avva; Sefarvayim = Sepharvaim; deity names Sukkot-Benot = Succoth-benoth, Nergal = Nergal, Ashima = Ashima, Nivchaz = Nibhaz, Tartaq = Tartak, Adrammelekh = Adrammelech, Anammelekh = Anammelech; gentilics 'the Shomronites' (haššōmərōnîm; ASV 'the Samaritans'), 'the Avvites', 'the Sefarvites'. Kept in English: Horeb, Gilgal, Asherah / Asherim, David. The drafts' 'Shomeron' and 'Mosheh' are normalized to Shomron and Moshe as in the existing table.
entries.rationale: Kings continues the narrative Hebrew of Genesis and Exodus, and the Wheel of Heaven Translation renders the Torah narrative books with transliterated name forms (genesis-woh: Avraham, Ya'aqov, Yosef, Beit-El, Be'er Sheva; exodus-woh: Yisra'el, Aharon, Ya'aqov), so the Kings narratives adopt the same practice rather than switching to the KJV forms used in the Latter-Prophets volumes (isaiah-woh, ezekiel-woh). The transliteration makes the theophoric element visible on the surface: Eliyahu ('my El is Yah'), Ovadyahu ('servant of Yah'), Achazyahu ('Yah has grasped') and Yehoram/Yehoshafat carry the Yahwistic name that the Elijah cycle sets against Ba'al, and the cycle's central confession at 1 Kgs 18:39 (YHWH hûʾ hāʾĕlōhîm) is a play on the prophet's own name (Cogan, 1 Kings, AB 10, 2001; Gray, I & II Kings, OTL). The MT writes the short forms ʾēliyyâ (2 Kgs 1:3, 4, 8, 12) and ʾăḥazyâ (2 Kgs 1:2) beside the long forms; both are standard variants of the same name (the short -yâ form predominates in post-exilic books), the ASV and all major versions normalize them, and the translation does likewise, recording the MT spelling in commentary. The Exodus exception ('Moses', 'Pharaoh') is a grandfathered single-book decision for two names whose English form is a household word; it is not extended here, because a mixed surface ('Elijah ... Ach'av ... Izevel') is less consistent than either pure option. This is a presentation convention with no interpretive content: every name is given with its conventional English equivalent in the table above and in the commentary at first occurrence in each chapter, so a reader can match the translation to the ASV and to the English editions of the Raëlian books, which quote these chapters as 'Elijah' and 'Elisha'. Founder preference point: the alternative (KJV forms throughout) is a mechanical substitution using the equivalence table and would require no other change. Ratified at human sign-off (2026-11-01, zarazinsfuss): Hebrew transliterated long forms with tz for tsade are kept book-wide, and each chapter title adds the English form of its principal name in parentheses, e.g. 'Eliyahu (Elijah)', for findability. Wave B (1 Kgs 1, 2, 13, 22) applies the same rules. The MT short forms ʾăḏōniyyâ and ṣiḏqiyyâ are normalized to the long forms, like ʾēliyyâ and ʾăḥazyâ in wave A, and the MT spelling is recorded in commentary at each site. Tsade is written tz, as in Tzarfat and Tzidon above and genesis-woh Yitzchaq; the wave-B draft's ts (Tseruyah, Tsadoq, Tsidqiyahu, Etsyon-Gever) is normalized. Gentilic adjectives take English '-ite' on the transliterated stem, as 'the Tishbite' and 'the Shunammite' already do, so David's guard hakkərēṯî wəhappəlēṯî (1 Kgs 1:38, 44) is 'the Kerethites and the Pelethites' (ASV 'Cherethites and Pelethites') and Barzillai and Shim'i are 'the Gil'adite' and 'the Binyaminite' (2:7, 8). Moshe (2:3) stays transliterated, because the exodus-woh 'Moses' is the grandfathered single-book exception described above. Waves C-D apply the tz rule to Mitzrayim and Tziyyon, which occur here for the first time in Kings; genesis-woh and exodus-woh print 'Mitsrayim' in their English lines (81 and 38 occurrences). Ratified at human sign-off (2026-11-01): Kings keeps 'Mitzrayim' under its tz rule; any corpus-wide normalization is a separate mechanical pass. Par'oh is transliterated like Moshe, since exodus-woh's 'Pharaoh' and 'Moses' are the grandfathered single-book exception. haššōmərōnîm (2 Kgs 17:29), the only occurrence of the word in the Hebrew Bible, is rendered 'the Shomronites' under the gentilic rule; the ASV 'the Samaritans' is anachronistic, because the word here means the Israelite inhabitants of Shomron, not the later Samaritan community (Cogan and Tadmor, II Kings, AB 11, 1988). The ASV's gentilic forms 'the Avvites' and 'the Sepharvites' (17:31) are matched by 'the Avvites' and 'the Sefarvites'. Month names are transliterated as in the ASV, and their later Babylonian equivalents are given in commentary.

entries.translit: hāʾĕlōhîm / ʾĕlōhîm / ʾĕlōhêḵem / ʾĕlōhê ʿeqrôn / kōh-yaʿăśûn ʾĕlōhîm
entries.partOfSpeech: noun, masculine plural; Kings application of the central elohim-as-translation convention
entries.literal: the god(s) / god(s) / your god(s) / the god(s) of Ekron / so may god(s) do
entries.standardEnglish: God (of YHWH); god / gods (of Baal, of Baal-zebub, in Jezebel's oath) - ASV
entries.wohChoice: (1) YHWH referent with the Hebrew article (hāʾĕlōhîm): 'the Elohim' (1 Kgs 18:21, 24, 37, 39; 19:8). (2) YHWH referent, anarthrous predicate or genitive: 'Elohim' without article ('that you are Elohim in Yisra'el', 18:36; 'no Elohim in Yisra'el', 2 Kgs 1:3, 6, 16; 'fire of Elohim', 2 Kgs 1:12). (3) Construct with a possessor: 'YHWH your/my Elohim', 'the Elohim of Yisra'el'. (4) Non-YHWH referent (Ba'al, Ba'al-Zevuv, the deities of Izevel's oath): lower-case 'elohim', number following the Hebrew agreement ('your elohim', 'he is an elohim', 'the elohim of Eqron', 'So may the elohim do' with the plural verbs yaʿăśûn / yôsipûn). Wave B under clause (2): 'May Elohim make' (1 Kgs 1:47, Qere ʾĕlōhîm) and the Israelite self-imprecation with a singular verb, sworn by YHWH, 'So may Elohim do to me, and more also' (1 Kgs 2:23). Waves C-D: clause (1) 'YHWH, he is the Elohim' (1 Kgs 8:60); clause (2) also covers an anarthrous subject in direct speech ('But will Elohim indeed dwell on the earth?', 8:27); clause (3) 'O Elohim of Yisra'el' in pure vocative without English article (8:26), and 'the Elohim of the land' (2 Kgs 17:26, 27), where the settlers speak of a territorial god but the narrator has identified the sender of the lions as YHWH (17:25); clause (4) 'other elohim' (2 Kgs 17:7, 35, 37, 38), 'elohim of its own', 'their own elohim', 'the elohim of Sefarvayim' (17:29, 31, 33). (5) Generic class in a comparison or negation: lower-case 'elohim' ('there is no elohim like you in the heavens above or on the earth beneath', 1 Kgs 8:23), because the referent is the class with which YHWH is compared, not YHWH.
entries.rationale: The central elohim-as-translation entry fixes the untranslated plural 'Elohim' and the narrative article; it was written for Genesis 1, where every occurrence refers to the one deity, and it does not say how to render the same lexeme when the Hebrew applies it to another god. Carmel (1 Kgs 18) is built on exactly that contrast: Eliyahu tells the Ba'al prophets to call on 'the name of your ʾĕlōhîm' (18:24, 25) and mocks Ba'al with kî-ʾĕlōhîm hûʾ 'for he is a god' (18:27), and the people's verdict is YHWH hûʾ hāʾĕlōhîm 'YHWH, he is the Elohim' (18:39); 2 Kgs 1 sets ʾĕlōhîm bəyiśrāʾēl against Ba'al-Zevuv ʾĕlōhê ʿeqrôn. Using one written form for both sides would erase the contrast the narrative depends on, and translating only the non-YHWH cases as 'god' would break the corpus decision to leave the lexeme untranslated, so the case distinction (capital for YHWH, lower case otherwise) follows the precedent of exodus-woh at Ex 20:3 ('other elohim', central elohim-aherim-other-gods-monolatry-vs-monotheism-scholarly-dispute-cross-corpus). The article follows the Hebrew where the Hebrew is anarthrous in predicate or genitive position (18:36 kî-ʾattâ ʾĕlōhîm; 2 Kgs 1:12 ʾēš-ʾĕlōhîm), because adding 'the' there would turn a classifying predicate ('that you are God in Israel', BDB ʾĕlōhîm 3) into an identification the Hebrew does not make; the narrative-subject article rule of the central entry is unaffected. Agreement also follows the Hebrew: Izevel's oath at 19:2 governs ʾĕlōhîm with plural verbs (as Ben-Hadad's oath does at 1 Kgs 20:10), unlike the same oath formula in Israelite mouths with singular verbs (1 Kgs 2:23; 1 Sam 3:17; 14:44; 2 Sam 3:9), so it is rendered as a plural 'the elohim'; the ASV's supplied 'to me' is not in the Hebrew of 19:2 and is not added. The capital/lower-case distinction is an editorial device, since Hebrew script has no case; the commentary states this at the first relevant verse. Clause (5) (wave C) follows from the referent principle of clause (4): in the incomparability formula ʾên-kāmôḵā ʾĕlōhîm (1 Kgs 8:23; cf. Ex 15:11 mî-ḵāmōḵā bāʾēlim; Ps 86:8 ʾên-kāmôḵā ḇāʾĕlōhîm) the noun classifies, and a capital would read as a name and make the sentence compare YHWH with himself. Whether the formula presupposes other divine beings or is monotheistic, as Deut 4:39 suggests, is not decided by the case, and the commentary says so; the ASV 'no God like thee' takes the monotheistic reading. At 2 Kgs 17:26-27 the case follows the referent as the narrator identifies it, not the speakers' theology, and the commentary records the ASV's lower-case 'god of the land'.

entries.partOfSpeech: construct noun phrase used as a prophetic title
entries.literal: man of the God / a man of God
entries.standardEnglish: man of God (ASV, KJV, NRSV, NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'man of the Elohim' where the Hebrew has the article (1 Kgs 17:18; 2 Kgs 1:9, 11, 12, 13); 'a man of Elohim' where it does not (1 Kgs 17:24; 2 Kgs 1:10); wave B: 'a man of Elohim' at 1 Kgs 13:1 and 'the man of the Elohim' at its fourteen articular occurrences (13:4, 5, 6 twice, 7, 8, 11, 12, 14 twice, 21, 26, 29, 31); waves C-D: 'the man of the Elohim' at the ten articular occurrences of 2 Kgs 4 (vv 7, 16, 21, 22, 25 twice, 27 twice, 40, 42) and 'a holy man of Elohim' at the anarthrous v 9
entries.rationale: ʾîš (hā)ʾĕlōhîm is the title Kings gives to Eliyahu, Elisha and the anonymous Judahite prophet of 1 Kgs 13; it designates a person who belongs to and acts for the deity, and it is used more in Kings than in any other book (BDB ʾîš 5; Cogan, 1 Kings, on 13:1). The central elohim-as-translation convention requires 'Elohim' to remain untranslated, so 'man of God' cannot be used without breaking the corpus decision; the remaining question is the article, and the Hebrew itself alternates. In 2 Kgs 1:9-13 the alternation carries meaning: the first two captains address Eliyahu with the articular title ʾîš hāʾĕlōhîm, Eliyahu answers the first with the anarthrous ʾim-ʾîš ʾĕlōhîm ʾānî 'if I am a man of God' (1:10), the second time with the articular form (1:12), and the narrator then calls the fire ʾēš-ʾĕlōhîm (1:12); the ʾîš / ʾēš wordplay ('man' / 'fire') is widely noted (Cogan and Tadmor, II Kings, AB 11, 1988). Following the Hebrew article keeps that alternation visible, which a uniform 'man of God' or 'man of Elohim' would hide. The woman's confession at 1 Kgs 17:24 (ʾîš ʾĕlōhîm ʾattâ), quoted in the English edition of the Raëlian canon as 'a man of God', is anarthrous and is rendered 'a man of Elohim'; the commentary gives the conventional English. In 1 Kgs 13 the title is anarthrous at its first occurrence (13:1) and articular at all fourteen later ones, where the article is anaphoric ('the man already mentioned'). Grammatically the article on the genitive makes the whole construct chain definite (GKC §127a; Joüon-Muraoka §139a), so 'the man of Elohim' would also be acceptable English; the convention nevertheless renders the Hebrew article where it stands, because the same written form carries meaning in 2 Kgs 1:9-13 and one rule for the whole book keeps the Hebrew auditable. The Raëlian canon quotes 13:1 in English as 'a man of God'; the conventional English is given in commentary.

entries.lemma: nepeš 'throat, breath, life, living being, self'
entries.wohChoice: 'nefesh' (transliterated, house spelling) only where the nepeš is named as the life-component that departs or returns (1 Kgs 17:21-22, governed by central tzet-nephesh-departure-at-death-formula); idiomatic English elsewhere: 'life' (19:2, 3, 4b, 10, 14; 2 Kgs 1:13-14), reflexive 'himself' (19:4a), and 'as you yourself live' for the oath ḥê-napšəḵā (2 Kgs 2:2, 4, 6); wave B: 'life' (1 Kgs 1:12; 1:29 'who has redeemed my life', ASV 'soul'; 2:23 'against his own life'), and 'being' in the Deuteronomic pair bəḵol-ləḇāḇām ûḇəḵol-napšām 'with all their heart and with all their being' (1 Kgs 2:4; ASV 'soul'); waves C-D: 'being' in the heart-and-nepeš pair (1 Kgs 8:48, as 2:4); 'she is in bitter distress' for the idiom nap̄šāh mārâ-lāh (2 Kgs 4:27; ASV 'her soul is vexed within her'); 'as you yourself live' for the oath ḥê-nap̄šəḵā (2 Kgs 4:30, as 2 Kgs 2:2, 4, 6)
entries.rationale: nepeš has a wide range (throat, breath, appetite, life, living being, the person him- or herself; HALOT nepeš 1-9; Wolff, Anthropology of the Old Testament, 1974), and the central glossary already rejects the Platonic 'soul' for it (nefesh-chayah) and transliterates it where it names the life that leaves the body at death (tzet-nephesh-departure-at-death-formula, which cites 1 Kgs 17:21-22 as the return-of-nepeš counterpart to Gen 35:18). In 1 Kgs 17:21-22 the nepeš of the boy 'returns into his inward part' (tāšāḇ ... ʿal-qirbô), so the noun names exactly that life-component and is transliterated; at every other site in the wave the word is part of an idiom ('to seek someone's nepeš' = to seek to kill; 'to go for one's nepeš' = to flee for one's life; wayyišʾal ʾeṯ-napšô lāmûṯ 'he asked for himself that he might die'; ḥê-napšəḵā 'by your life'), where English 'life' or a reflexive renders the idiom accurately and a transliteration would suggest a technical sense that is not there. The oath ḥay-YHWH wəḥê-napšəḵā (2 Kgs 2:2, 4, 6; also 1 Sam 1:26; 20:3; 25:26; 2 Kgs 4:30) swears by YHWH's life and the addressee's life; 'as you yourself live' (cf. NJPS 'as you live') keeps the second oath-member without the ASV's 'soul', in line with nefesh-chayah. Spelling: the central glossary uses 'nefesh' in nefesh-chayah, nefesh-blessing-transfer, karet-penalty-cut-off-from-people and shivim-nefesh, and 'nephesh' only in tzet-nephesh; 'nefesh' (f for the spirantized p, as in Yosef, Shafat, Yehoshafat) is the house spelling, and a central diff proposes normalizing tzet-nephesh's wohChoice accordingly. In wave B, pāḏâ ʾeṯ-napšî at 1 Kgs 1:29 (the rescue idiom of David's oath, also 2 Sam 4:9) takes 'life', and the Deuteronomic heart-and-nepeš pair at 2:4 (Deut 6:5) takes 'being', the whole living self (HALOT nepeš 'person, self'; Wolff 1974; Alter's rendering of Deut 6:5), not the ASV 'soul'. Later Kings waves should use the same pair at 1 Kgs 8:48 and 2 Kgs 23:3, 25. mar-nepeš 'bitter of nepeš' (1 Sam 1:10; 22:2; Judg 18:25; 2 Kgs 4:27) is an idiom for acute distress and is rendered in plain English (NRSV, NJPS 'she is in bitter distress'), with the literal form given in commentary. 1 Kgs 8:48 applies the wave-B rendering of the Deuteronomic pair, as the wave-B extension anticipated.

entries.source: רוּחַ יְהוָה / רוּחַ אֵלִיָּהוּ / רוּחַ גְּדוֹלָה
entries.translit: rûaḥ YHWH / rûaḥ ʾēliyyāhû / rûaḥ gədôlâ
entries.literal: the wind/breath/spirit of YHWH; the spirit of Elijah; a great wind
entries.standardEnglish: the Spirit of Jehovah (1 Kgs 18:12; 2 Kgs 2:16 ASV); thy spirit / the spirit of Elijah (2 Kgs 2:9, 15); a great and strong wind (1 Kgs 19:11)
entries.wohChoice: 'the ruach of YHWH' where rûaḥ YHWH is an agent that carries the prophet off (1 Kgs 18:12; 2 Kgs 2:16), and 'ruach' for the prophet's rûaḥ that passes from Eliyahu to Elisha (2 Kgs 2:9, 15), so the same Hebrew word stays visible across 2 Kgs 2:9-16; 'wind' where the context is plainly meteorological (rûaḥ gədôlâ wəḥāzāq, 1 Kgs 19:11 three times); and 'the ruach of YHWH' also where rûaḥ YHWH is the inspiring agent a prophet claims to speak by (1 Kgs 22:24, Tzidqiyahu's retort), the sense of the prophet's rûaḥ at 2 Kgs 2:9, 15. The council figure hārûaḥ and the rûaḥ šeqer of 1 Kgs 22:21-23 are governed by the 1-kings-woh entry ha-ruach-ruach-sheqer-the-ruach-and-the-lying-ruach-1-kings-22
entries.rationale: rûaḥ covers 'wind', 'breath' and 'spirit' (BDB; HALOT rûaḥ 1-11), and in the two Elijah passages where rûaḥ YHWH is said to carry a prophet away (1 Kgs 18:12, 'the rûaḥ YHWH will carry you I know not where'; 2 Kgs 2:16, 'lest the rûaḥ YHWH has taken him up and cast him on one of the mountains') commentators divide between a divine 'spirit' and a 'wind of YHWH' (cf. Isa 40:7; Hos 13:15, where rûaḥ YHWH is a wind; Gray, I & II Kings, OTL; Cogan and Tadmor, II Kings, AB 11). The ASV capital 'Spirit' settles the ambiguity in favour of the later doctrinal concept of a personal Holy Spirit, which the Hebrew does not specify; the corpus precedent for a rûaḥ that physically transports a prophet is ezekiel-woh, which renders rûaḥ YHWH 'the ruach of YHWH' at Ezek 37:1 (cf. central ruach-chayyot, also inferred), and the Kings wave follows it. In 2 Kgs 2 the narrative links the rûaḥ that Elisha asks for (2:9) and that the prophets see resting on him (2:15) with the rûaḥ YHWH they fear has carried Eliyahu off (2:16), right after an ascent in a storm (2:11); a single transliterated term keeps that verbal link visible, which 'spirit' / 'Spirit' / 'wind' in three different places would break. Where the Hebrew is unambiguously meteorological (the wind that tears the mountains at Horeb, 1 Kgs 19:11) the word is translated 'wind', consistent with the central ruach-gedolah-midbar treatment. The entry is inferred, not direct: transliteration is a decision to leave a recognized ambiguity unresolved, and the 'wind' reading of rûaḥ YHWH at 18:12 and 2:16 is defensible but a minority view; the commentary sets out both readings and does not choose between them. At 1 Kgs 22:24 Tzidqiyahu asks 'Which way did the rûaḥ-YHWH pass from me to speak to you?', answering Mikhayehu's report that a rûaḥ of the council has become 'a lying rûaḥ' in the prophets' mouths (22:21-23); the retort only works if the reader sees the same noun, so the transliteration applies here too, and the ASV capital 'Spirit of Jehovah' is not used for the same reason as at 1 Kgs 18:12.

entries.lemma: Ketiv ('what is written', the consonantal text) and Qere ('what is read', the Masoretic reading tradition)
entries.literal: the written consonants vs the vocalized reading
entries.standardEnglish: ASV and all major English versions translate the Qere silently
entries.wohChoice: translate the Qere; record the Ketiv in commentary at every site. Wave A sites: 1 Kgs 17:14 (K tittēn / Q tēt), 17:15 (K 'he and she' / Q 'she and he'), 18:36 (K 'your words' / Q 'your word'), 18:42 (K defective / Q birkāyw 'his knees'), 19:4 (K fem. ʾaḥat / Q masc. ʾeḥād), 2 Kgs 2:16 (K / Q 'the valleys', orthographic). Wave B sites (seven readings in six verses): 1 Kgs 1:27 (K 'your servants' / Q 'your servant'), 1:37 (K jussive yhy / Q yihyeh), 1:47 (K 'your Elohim' / Q 'Elohim'), 2:24 (K plene / Q wayyôšîḇanî, orthographic), 22:13 (K 'your words' / Q 'your word'), 22:49 (K ʿśr / Q ʿāśâ 'made'; K nšbrh / Q nišbərû 'were broken'). Waves C-D sites (22 readings in 19 verses): 1 Kgs 6:5, 6, 10 (K yṣwʿ / Q yāṣîaʿ 'side-structure'), 6:16 and 6:21 (orthographic), 6:38 (K singular / Q plural 'its specifications'), 8:26 (K 'your words' / Q 'your word'), 8:48 (K bnyt / Q bānîṯî 'I have built'); 2 Kgs 4:2, 3, 7 (twice), 16, 23 (twice) (archaic 2nd feminine singular forms in the Ketiv), 4:5 (participle form), 4:34 (K 'his palm' / Q 'his palms'); 17:13 (K 'his prophets' / Q 'prophets of'), 17:16 (K absolute / Q construct 'two'), 17:21 (K wydʾ / Q wayyaddaḥ 'drove away'), 17:31 (K ʾlh sprym / Q ʾĕlōhê səp̄arwāyim)
entries.rationale: The Leningrad Codex marks each Ketiv/Qere pair with the Qere vocalization placed on the Ketiv consonants (or in the margin), and the Masoretic tradition reads the Qere; English Bible translation, including the ASV baseline, follows the Qere in all but a handful of cases (Tov, Textual Criticism of the Hebrew Bible, 3rd ed., 2012, on Ketiv/Qere). None of the six wave-A pairs changes the sense materially: two are grammatical (17:14 finite verb vs infinitive construct; 19:4 gender agreement with rōṯem, which is masculine in 19:5), two are number variants (18:36 'words'/'word'; 18:42 defective spelling of 'his knees'), one is word order (17:15) and one orthographic (2 Kgs 2:16). Translating the Qere keeps the English aligned with the reading tradition and with every major version, while recording the Ketiv in the commentary keeps the consonantal text auditable. The same rule is the project baseline in genesis-woh and exodus-woh; this entry makes it explicit for Kings so later waves can extend the appliesTo list. Of the seven wave-B readings, two depart from the ASV, which follows the Ketiv at 1 Kgs 1:27 ('thy servants') and 1:47 ('Thy God'); the Qere is translated there as everywhere, and the ASV reading is recorded in commentary. In waves C-D the ASV follows the Ketiv at 1 Kgs 6:38 ('according to all the fashion of it'); elsewhere it agrees with the Qere. The Ketiv forms of 2 Kgs 4 (-kî, ʾattî) are archaic or northern second-person feminine forms characteristic of the Elisha stories (Rendsburg, Israelian Hebrew in the Book of Kings, 2002) and do not affect the sense. Where the Qere stands at verse end (2 Kgs 4:5; 17:31) the source edition places the sof pasuq inside the bracketed Qere in the Hebrew text field; the text is kept as delivered.

entries.source: מִתֹּשָׁבֵי גִלְעָד ; חֲמִשִּׁים אִישׁ ; וַיַּרְא ; שְׁלִשִׁים ; אַף־הוּא ...
entries.translit: mittōšāḇê gilʿāḏ ; ḥămiššîm ʾîš ; wayyarʾ ; šəlišîm ; ʾap̄-hûʾ ...
entries.lemma: Masoretic vocalization and division where the ancient versions (LXX, Peshitta, Vulgate) or modern emendations read otherwise
entries.literal: the MT as vocalized and divided
entries.standardEnglish: ASV follows the MT at these sites; NRSV and some modern versions adopt the versional reading at 1 Kgs 17:1 and 19:3
entries.wohChoice: translate the MT vocalization and verse division; give the versional reading in commentary. Sites: 1 Kgs 17:1 'of the settlers of Gil'ad' (MT mittōšāḇê; LXX ek Thesbōn 'from Tishbe'); 18:4 'fifty men to a cave' (MT singular ḥămiššîm ʾîš; LXX/Peshitta distributive as in 18:13); 18:26 impersonal 'which was given them ... which had been made' (MT singular active verbs); 19:3 'And he saw' (MT wayyarʾ; LXX/Peshitta/Vulgate 'he was afraid', wayyîrāʾ); 2 Kgs 1:13 'the captain of a third fifty' (MT plural šəlišîm); 2 Kgs 2:14 ʾap̄-hûʾ opening the second half, as the major disjunctive on ʾēliyyāhû divides the verse (so also ASV; LXX aphphō is the alternative). Versification: 1 Kgs 18:33-34 follows the MT division (MT 18:34 = ASV 18:33b-34). Wave B sites: 1 Kgs 1:8 'and Re'i' (MT proper name; some Greek witnesses 'his companions'); 1:18 second wəʿattâ 'and now' (many MSS and versions wəʾattâ 'and you', ASV); 1:40 'split' (LXX 'resounded'); 2:22 the elliptical 'even for him, and for Evyatar ...'; 2:28 'after Avshalom' (versions 'after Shelomoh'); 2:29 (LXX plus) and 2:35, 46 (LXX supplements 2:35a-o, 2:46a-l, not translated); 13:11 'his son' (versions 'his sons'); 13:12 'had seen' (versions Hiphil 'showed him'); 22:6 ʾăḏōnāy 'the Lord' (many MSS YHWH); 22:28 'Hear, you peoples, all of you' (absent from LXX; = Mic 1:2; translated, noted as a probable addition); 22:38 (LXX adds the pigs and 'in the blood'). Versification: 1 Kgs 22:21-22 (MT v 21 ends with 'By what means?', which English versions place at the start of v 22) and 22:43-54 (MT 22:43-44 = ASV 22:43; MT 22:45-54 = ASV 22:44-53; MT 1 Kings has 54 verses in ch. 22). Waves C-D sites: 1 Kgs 6:1 'four hundred and eightieth' (LXX 440, followed by 6:1a–d carrying MT 5:31–32 and 6:37–38; Rahlfs); 6:8 'the middle side-chamber' (LXX 'the lowest'); 6:11-14 (absent from LXX Vaticanus; translated); 6:15 'the walls of the ceiling' (LXX 'beams', qôrôṯ); 6:20 'covered the altar' (LXX 'made an altar'); 6:34 qəlāʿîm construed 'leaves' (BDB), where most read ṣəlāʿîm; 8:1-5 (LXX shorter text); 8:12-13 (LXX places a longer form after 8:53, ending 'in the book of the song'); 8:16 (LXX and 2 Chr 6:5-6 longer; probable homoioteleuton in the MT); 8:31 second ʾālâ construed as the verb 'and swears' (ASV, LXX), no emendation; 8:37 'in the land of their cities' (MT 'land of his gates'; LXX 'in one of'); 8:65 'seven days and seven days, fourteen days' (LXX 'seven days'); 2 Kgs 17:27 plural verbs followed by singular 'let him teach' (versions harmonize).
entries.rationale: The Wheel of Heaven Translation translates the Masoretic Text and records ancient-version and conjectural readings in the apparatus rather than adopting them in the line; this is the baseline of genesis-woh (e.g., yov-yashuv at Gen 46:13) and exodus-woh (kes-yah-vs-nes-yah at Ex 17:16). At each wave-A site the MT gives a construable sense: 'of the settlers of Gil'ad' is grammatical, if repetitive after 'the Tishbite' (Burney, Notes on the Hebrew Text of the Books of Kings, 1903); wayyarʾ 'he saw' makes sense as 'he saw (how things stood)', even though most moderns prefer the versional 'he was afraid' (Cogan, 1 Kings, AB 10); the singular verbs at 18:26 can be impersonal; šəlišîm at 2 Kgs 1:13 can be read as 'a third (set)' (Cogan and Tadmor, II Kings, AB 11). Because the MT can be construed at each site, emending it would be a textual-critical decision beyond the remit of a translation that commits to the MT; the alternatives are given in commentary so the reader can see where the major versions differ. Verse numbers follow the Hebrew (the chapter files are keyed to MT refIds); at 1 Kgs 18:33-34 the English versions divide the verses one clause earlier, and the commentary records the difference so that canon or ASV citations by verse number can be matched.

entries.literal: YHWH of armies/hosts; YHWH, God of armies/hosts
entries.standardEnglish: Jehovah of hosts; Jehovah, the God of hosts (ASV)
entries.wohChoice: 'YHWH of hosts' (1 Kgs 18:15); 'YHWH, the Elohim of hosts' (1 Kgs 19:10, 14)
entries.rationale: The title is rendered as in the isaiah-woh overlay entry yhwh-tzevaot-hosts-isaiah ('YHWH of hosts'), keeping the corpus divine-name style 'YHWH' and the ASV noun 'hosts', so the title reads the same in Kings and in Isaiah. The construction YHWH ṣəḇāʾôṯ (a proper name in apparent construct) is grammatically debated, and the referent of the 'hosts' (Israel's armies, the heavenly host, the divine assembly) is disputed (Mettinger, The Dethronement of Sabaoth, 1982; Cross, Canaanite Myth and Hebrew Epic, 1973); 'hosts' is the conventional English that leaves both senses open, where 'armies' would narrow it. The expanded form at 19:10, 14 (YHWH ʾĕlōhê ṣəḇāʾôṯ) contains ʾĕlōhîm in construct with a possessor and is rendered by the elohim-referent-and-article-conventions-kings rule ('the Elohim of hosts'). No transliteration 'Tseva'ot' is introduced, so as not to set the Kings volumes apart from the existing Isaiah rendering.

entries.lemma: baʿal 'owner, lord, husband'; as a divine name, the West-Semitic storm god Baal
entries.partOfSpeech: divine name (normally with the article in Hebrew prose); plural for local manifestations or images
entries.wohChoice: 'Ba'al' without the English article (1 Kgs 18:19, 21, 22, 25, 26, 40; 19:18); plural 'the Ba'als' (18:18); compound divine names hyphenated and transliterated ('Ba'al-Zevuv', 2 Kgs 1); 'And he served Ba'al' (1 Kgs 22:54, MT ʾeṯ-habbaʿal); 'and served Ba'al' (2 Kgs 17:16, MT ʾeṯ-habbaʿal; draft 'Baal' aligned with the Kings spelling)
entries.rationale: Hebrew prose regularly writes the god's name with the article (habbaʿal), a remnant of its origin as the title 'the Lord'; English treats the word as a proper name, and the ASV, NRSV and NJPS all omit the article, so the translation does likewise and records the Hebrew article here and in commentary. The spelling Ba'al with the apostrophe for ʿayin follows the genesis-woh transliteration practice (cf. Ba'al-Chanan, Gen 36:38) and the hebrew-proper-name-transliteration-convention-kings entry. The Ugaritic deity is governed by the central baal-ugaritic-baalu-storm-god-cross-corpus-hebrew-bible-polemic entry, whose wohChoice ('Baʿlu') is limited to Ugaritic sources; this entry is its Hebrew-Bible counterpart and records that the Carmel narrative (rain withheld and restored, fire from the sky) is widely read as a polemic against Baal's storm-god attributes (Cogan, 1 Kings, AB 10; Smith, The Early History of God, 2nd ed., 2002). The plural habbəʿālîm (18:18) denotes local Baal cults or images and is rendered 'the Ba'als' (ASV 'the Baalim').

entries.lemma: baʿal 'lord' + zəḇûḇ 'fly'; divine name of the deity of Ekron
entries.partOfSpeech: divine name in apposition with a construct title
entries.literal: Lord of the fly / flies, the god of Ekron
entries.wohChoice: 'Ba'al-Zevuv, the elohim of Eqron' (MT form transliterated; lower-case elohim per elohim-referent-and-article-conventions-kings)
entries.rationale: The MT name baʿal zəḇûḇ means 'Lord of the fly/flies' (LXX Baal muian theon 'Baal-fly god'); many scholars hold that it deforms an original baʿal zəḇûl 'Baal the Prince', since zbl bʿl 'Prince Baal' is a standard Ugaritic epithet and the New Testament has Beelzeboul (Mark 3:22) (Cogan and Tadmor, II Kings, AB 11, 1988; Day, Yahweh and the Gods and Goddesses of Canaan, 2000). Others take 'Lord of flies' as a genuine cult title of a healing or oracular god (cf. Greek Zeus Apomyios), so the deformation hypothesis is likely but not certain. The translation keeps the MT form, which is the text being translated and which the narrative repeats four times (1:2, 3, 6, 16), and puts the reconstruction in commentary, following mt-baseline-at-versional-cruxes-and-versification-kings. The construct title ʾĕlōhê ʿeqrôn takes lower-case 'elohim' because the referent is not YHWH, which keeps the contrast with the refrain 'is there no Elohim in Yisra'el?' (1:3, 6, 16).

entries.lemma: bēn 'son'; in construct with a group noun, 'member of'
entries.standardEnglish: the sons of the prophets (ASV, KJV, NJPS 'disciples of the prophets' in some places); company of prophets (NRSV)
entries.wohChoice: 'the sons of the prophets' (ASV preserved; the membership sense explained in commentary)
entries.rationale: bēn in construct with a group noun commonly means 'member of' rather than 'descendant of' (bənê-yiśrāʾēl, bən-ʾāḏām; GKC §128v; BDB bēn 7), so bənê-hannəḇîʾîm are members of a prophetic group, not children of prophets. The term is almost confined to the Elisha narratives (1 Kgs 20:35; 2 Kgs 2:3-15; 4:1, 38; 5:22; 6:1; 9:1), where the groups live together, eat together and address Elisha as 'master' (Wilson, Prophecy and Society in Ancient Israel, 1980). 'Company/guild of prophets' (NRSV) states the sense but loses the Hebrew idiom; keeping the ASV form and explaining it in commentary leaves the idiom visible and is consistent with the corpus's 'children of Yisra'el' for bənê yiśrāʾēl.

entries.lemma: peh 'mouth; portion, share' in construct with šənayim 'two'
entries.standardEnglish: a double portion (ASV, KJV, NJPS); a double share (NRSV)
entries.rationale: pî-šənayim is the legal term for the firstborn's inheritance in Deut 21:17, where the firstborn receives 'a share of two' of the father's property, i.e., twice what each other son receives; Elisha asks to be Eliyahu's principal heir, not to have twice Eliyahu's power (Cogan and Tadmor, II Kings, AB 11; Gray, I & II Kings, OTL). The same phrase means 'two-thirds' in Zech 13:8, and some interpreters have read it so here, but the inheritance context (Elisha calls Eliyahu 'my father' in 2:12) favours the Deuteronomy sense. 'A double portion' is the conventional English and is accurate for the inheritance sense; the alternatives are noted in commentary. The object of the inheritance is rûaḥ, governed by ruach-yhwh-and-prophetic-ruach-transliteration-kings.

entries.source: רֶכֶב־אֵשׁ וְסוּסֵי אֵשׁ ; רֶכֶב יִשְׂרָאֵל וּפָרָשָׁיו
entries.translit: rekeḇ-ʾēš wəsûsê ʾēš ; rekeḇ yiśrāʾēl ûp̄ārāšāyw
entries.lemma: rekeḇ 'chariot; chariotry (collective)'; sûs 'horse'; ʾēš 'fire'; pārāš 'horseman' or 'horse'
entries.literal: chariot(ry) of fire and horses of fire; the chariot(ry) of Israel and its horsemen
entries.standardEnglish: there appeared a chariot of fire, and horses of fire (ASV, with 'there appeared' supplied); the chariots of Israel and the horsemen thereof (ASV 2:12)
entries.wohChoice: 'a chariot of fire and horses of fire' (2:11, literal construct chains, nothing supplied); 'the chariots of Yisra'el and its horsemen' (2:12, ASV)
entries.rationale: The Hebrew of 2:11 is a verbless presentative clause (wəhinnēh rekeḇ-ʾēš wəsûsê ʾēš) followed by a plural verb (wayyaprîḏû bên šənêhem 'and they separated the two of them'); the translation keeps the construct chains and the plural verb and does not supply the ASV's 'there appeared', which is not in the Hebrew. rekeḇ is the same singular form in 2:11 and 2:12; it can be a single chariot or collective 'chariotry', and the ASV's 'a chariot' / 'the chariots' reflects that range; the translation keeps the ASV and notes in commentary that the lexeme is identical, since Elisha's cry 'the chariots of Yisra'el and its horsemen' is a fixed epithet (repeated for Elisha himself at 2 Kgs 13:14) describing the prophet as Israel's real military strength (Cogan and Tadmor, II Kings, AB 11; von Rad, Old Testament Theology II). pārāšîm can mean 'horsemen' or 'horses/steeds' (HALOT pārāš); the ASV 'horsemen' is kept. The fire-chariot and horses recur at 2 Kgs 6:17 as the heavenly army around Elisha, and divine chariots belong to the wider storm-theophany imagery (Ps 68:18; 104:3; Hab 3:8). The verse is the central Kings citation of the Raëlian canon (The Book Which Tells the Truth, ch. 3), which reads it as the departure of a flying craft; that reading is recorded only as a labelled reception note in the commentary, and the line itself renders the Hebrew literally without technical vocabulary.

entries.lemma: ghr 'bend down, crouch' (Qal; three occurrences, all in Kings)
entries.standardEnglish: bowed himself down / cast himself down (1 Kgs 18:42, ASV / KJV); stretched himself upon (2 Kgs 4:34-35, ASV, KJV); crouched, bent over (modern versions)
entries.wohChoice: 'he crouched down upon the earth' (1 Kgs 18:42, wave A); 'he crouched over him' (2 Kgs 4:34, 35)
entries.rationale: *gāhar* occurs only three times, all in the Elijah-Elisha cycle: Eliyahu on Karmel, praying for rain with his face between his knees (1 Kgs 18:42), and Elisha over the dead boy at Shunem (2 Kgs 4:34, 35). The lexica give 'bend down, crouch' (BDB; HALOT), a sense that fits a posture with the face between the knees, and the ASV renders the three sites with two different verbs ('bowed himself down', 'stretched himself upon'), the second taking its sense from the preceding 'lay upon the child'. The wave-A line already reads 'he crouched down' at 1 Kgs 18:42, and its commentary points to 2 Kgs 4:34-35; using the same verb at all three sites keeps visible the link between the two prophets' intercessory postures, which the narrative draws deliberately (Elisha's raising of the Shunammite's son repeats Eliyahu's at Tzarfat, 1 Kgs 17:17-24 // 2 Kgs 4:18-37; Cogan and Tadmor, *II Kings*, AB 11, 1988). The entry is a concordance decision with no interpretive content; the canon's reading of 2 Kgs 4:32-37 as a resuscitation is recorded only in a labelled reception note. Application note: the wave-A chapter paragraph 1KI-WOH-18:42 should receive this id in glossaryRefs when the overlay diff is applied.

entries.partOfSpeech: noun, feminine singular (with article in 2 Kgs 17:13, 34, 37)
entries.standardEnglish: law (ASV, KJV, NRSV); Teaching (NJPS); torah (exodus-woh at Ex 13:9; 16:4)
entries.wohChoice: 'the law' in Kings: 'the law of Moshe' (1 Kgs 2:3, wave B); 'according to all the law' (2 Kgs 17:13); 'the law ... the commandment' (17:34, 37)
entries.rationale: *tôrâ* ranges from a parent's or priest's instruction to a body of written law (BDB; HALOT). In the Deuteronomistic History it names the written law of Moshe, the Deuteronomic book (Deut 31:9-12, 24-26; Josh 1:7-8; 1 Kgs 2:3; 2 Kgs 14:6; 17:37 'which he wrote for you'; 22:8-11), and it stands in fixed series with *ḥuqqîm* 'statutes', *mišpāṭîm* 'ordinances' and *miṣwâ* 'commandment' (2 Kgs 17:34, 37). In that usage the ASV 'law' is accurate and is kept, as the wave-B Editor already did at 1 Kgs 2:3 (von Rad, *Studies in Deuteronomy*, 1953; Weinfeld, *Deuteronomy and the Deuteronomic School*, 1972). exodus-woh renders *tôrâ* 'torah' (Ex 13:9 'the torah of YHWH'; 16:4) without a glossary entry; the transliteration there suits the earlier, broader sense of 'instruction', and the difference between the two books is one of register, not of meaning. This entry records the Kings decision so that a later corpus-wide entry can reconcile the two; whether to unify the rendering is a founder point in the wave-C/D editor report. Within 2 Kgs 17 'law' is reserved for *tôrâ*, and the customary-practice sense of *mišpāṭ* is rendered 'manner' (2-kings-woh `mishpat-manner-custom-2-kings-17`). Application note: the wave-B paragraph 1KI-WOH-2:3 should receive this id in glossaryRefs when the overlay diff is applied.

entries.lemma: mišpāṭ 'judgement, justice; legal claim; ordinance; custom, manner'
entries.partOfSpeech: noun, masculine singular and plural (construct and with suffixes)
entries.standardEnglish: law (2 Kgs 17:26-27, ASV, NRSV); manner (17:26-27, KJV; 17:33, 34, 40, ASV); ordinances (17:34b, 37, ASV); rules (17:26-27, NJPS)
entries.wohChoice: 'manner' where mišpāṭ is the customary practice of a people or of a territorial god: 'the manner of the Elohim of the land' (2 Kgs 17:26 twice, 27), 'the manner of the nations' (17:33), 'the former manners' (17:34a), 'their former manner' (17:40); 'ordinances' in the legal series with ḥuqqîm / tôrâ / miṣwâ (17:34b, 37)
entries.rationale: *mišpāṭ* has a wide range, from 'judgement' and 'legal claim' (1 Kgs 8:45, 49, 59 'their cause') to 'ordinance' and 'custom, manner, regular practice' (BDB *mišpāṭ* 6; HALOT; Judg 18:7; 1 Sam 8:9-11; 2 Kgs 1:7 'what manner of man'). 2 Kgs 17:24-41 uses it as a keyword: the settlers do not know the *mišpāṭ* of the god of the land (vv 26-27), they serve their own gods according to the *mišpāṭ* of the nations (v 33), and later generations still follow 'the former *mišpāṭîm*' (vv 34, 40) instead of the statutes, ordinance, *tôrâ* and commandment given to Yaʿaqov (vv 34, 37). The ASV renders the first sites 'law' and the later ones 'manner', which hides the repetition and gives 'law' to both *mišpāṭ* and *tôrâ* in the same passage; the KJV has 'manner' throughout vv 26-40. The translation follows the KJV at vv 26-27, so that the customary-practice sense is rendered 'manner' consistently and 'law' is reserved for *tôrâ* (`torah-law-deuteronomistic-kings`), while the legal-series sense keeps 'ordinances' as in 1 Kgs 6:12 and 8:58 (on the keyword structure of the passage, Cogan and Tadmor, *II Kings*, AB 11, 1988). The decision is concordance-driven and has no interpretive content.
